summary:
Global population growth is increasing the demand for food, while agriculture already accounts for a large share of freshwater use. Meeting this demand sustainably calls for smarter, data-informed farming. Precision agriculture uses information technologies to help farmers respond to field conditions and manage resources more effectively. Research has demonstrated the potential of machine learning in agricultural applications: for example, Espejo-García et al. (2020) explored transfer learning to support weed identification and reported F1 scores above 95% for several approaches. This provides a relevant precedent for applying machine learning in agriculture, though it does not directly validate crop-rotation recommendations.

Kayena is a crop-rotation decision-support tool that combines two perspectives: satellite data and measurements from the field. A Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM), trained on  NASA POWER data, runs on an ESP32 microcontroller connected to an in-field temperature and humidity sensor. The system classifies field conditions in real time, compares local measurements with satellite data, flags unusual conditions, and suggests three crop-rotation strategies—including the farmer’s current rotation—with supporting evidence, benefits, and risks.

Designed to work offline, Jackson aims to support farmers’ decisions rather than replace their judgment. Its recommendations should be validated in real field conditions across different crops, soils, and climates.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Kayena helps farmers understand the climate of their plot and plan their crop rotation. It works in three parts:

  1. Training with NASA data. We used 10 years (2016–2025) of daily NASA POWER climate data for Namiquipa, Chihuahua: 2016–2023 to train a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) and 2024–2025 to test it on years it had never seen. The model uses only air temperature and relative humidity. To choose the number of climate groups and their shape, we used the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC). The BIC scores each model on how well it explains the data and penalizes every extra parameter, so it picks the simplest model that still describes the climate well. The result was three groups, which we identified as the dry season, the rainy season and the cold-humid season. The model found these seasons without ever seeing rainfall data.
  2. On-field inference with TinyML. The trained model is exported as a C header file and runs on an ESP32 connected to a DHT11 sensor. The whole model is just a few dozen numbers, small enough to fit easily in the microcontroller's memory. The device classifies the plot's climate on the spot, without internet, and reports how sure it is of each result.
  3. An app for the farmer. The ESP32 sends its readings to a desktop app over Wi-Fi (or USB). The app averages 24 hours of readings to match the daily resolution of NASA's data and shows the current climate group. A Markov chain estimates the most likely climate group for the coming week, and the app warns of crop risks such as frost, cold, heat, fungi and dry spells. Based on what was planted before, it suggests options for the next crop in the rotation.

What are its benefits?

  • It turns global satellite data into concrete information for a single plot.
  • It works without internet, which is key in rural areas with poor connectivity.
  • It keeps a record of plantings, harvests and readings to track the rotation over time.
  • Along with the climate group, it reports the probability of each group, so the farmer can see how sure the model is.

What is the intended impact?

We want to support farmers' decisions. Climate information is now scattered or hard to access, and the tool puts it in one place at the moment it is needed. Farmers can complement their own experience and knowledge of the land with NASA data and prepare in advance for frost, heat or long dry seasons. The readings stored at each plot can also be used to retrain the model and adapt it to other regions.

Tools, programming languages, hardware and software

  • Data: NASA POWER daily air temperature and relative humidity (model inputs) and precipitation (used only to interpret the groups, not for training).
  • Training: Python with pandas and scikit-learn.
  • Hardware: ESP32 and DHT11 sensor.
  • Firmware: C/C++ in the Arduino IDE.
  • App: Go, with a local web interface that works offline.
  • Data capture: Python with pyserial, to log and compare sensor readings.

How is the project creative?

  • The GMM is an unsupervised model. It groups days by how similar they are in temperature and humidity, without being told in advance which season each day belongs to. The team then interpreted each group using the months and NASA's rainfall records. The groups matched the region's real seasons, even though the model never saw any rainfall data.
  • It connects historical satellite climate data with what happens on the plot: global data trains the model, local data drives the decision.
  • The intelligence lives on the microcontroller itself, not in the cloud.
  • It combines classification (GMM), forecasting (Markov chain) and agronomic knowledge (crop rotation rules from [SOURCE, e.g. INIFAP / FAO]) in a single tool.

What factors did the team consider?

  • What the field actually needs. We designed the tool with feedback from a local producer.
  • The model only uses what the sensor can measure. That is why we trained it only on air temperature and relative humidity.
  • Honesty about the model.
  • We evaluated it on years not used for training (2016–2025) and compared it against a simple human-written rule. The GMM matched the season labels [X]% of the time, versus [Y]% for the rule.
  • Offline by design. Everything works without internet.
  • Clear limitations. The DHT11 measures air, not soil, and only reads between 0 and 50 °C. Since it cannot detect frost directly, the app relies on the Markov forecast to warn about it. A wider-range sensor can replace it without retraining the model. The suggestions do not replace a soil analysis or technical advice.
